title: The Necessary Aftermath
premise: Elodie Eastwick, once a celebrated piano prodigy, returns to the Ashgrove Conservatory as a janitor, hiding in plain sight from a family that destroyed their career to protect a secret. When a box of undelivered letters surfaces behind a wardrobe in the old practice wing, Elodie discovers correspondence from students who were quietly expelled after accusing the conservatory's beloved founder of abuse—letters Elodie's own mother helped bury. As Elodie traces the letter-writers and confronts what their silence purchased, they must decide whether to expose the truth and lose the last fragile connection to their family, or remain invisible forever. The novel ends with Elodie reading the letters aloud at a memorial concert, choosing witness over survival, as the conservatory's board resigns and Elodie finally plays again.
about_author: Ada Delacroix is the pen name of a former classical musician who spent a decade teaching before turning to fiction. Her work examines institutions that protect themselves at the expense of the people inside them.

chapters.title: Tenant
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. We follow a night shift at Ashgrove Conservatory: mopping practice-room floors beneath posters of Elodie's own teenage face from a competition twenty years ago. A young violinist mistakes them for staff, then for nobody at all. The emotional beat is the strange comfort of being unseen—and the first flicker of grief that invisibility was a choice someone else made for them.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Clearing out the condemned practice wing, Elodie finds a box wedged behind a wardrobe: dozens of letters, stamped, sealed, never delivered, all addressed to the conservatory board between 1998 and 2003. One envelope bears Elodie's childhood address. The beat is vertigo—the past physically surfacing through the floorboards of the present.

chapters.title: Mother Tongue
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Elodie in the present, flashbacks to age fourteen. Elodie calls their mother under a pretext; the conversation is warm, rehearsed, evasive. Flashback reveals the night Elodie withdrew from the Tchaikovsky youth finals and the family rearranged itself around the word 'burnout.' The beat is the tenderness and violence of a shared lie.

chapters.title: Correspondents
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Researching return addresses, Elodie locates two surviving letter-writers: Ruth Okafor, now a music therapist in Leeds, and Tomas Beck, who never played again. Ruth agrees to meet but warns: 'You were the reason we wrote. You were also the reason it stopped.' The beat is the dawning horror that Elodie's career was the shield behind which others were silenced.

chapters.title: Founder's Day
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge at the conservatory's centenary celebration honoring Director Ambrose Vane, now elderly and revered. Elodie serves canapés while trustees toast 'a man who built futures.' Ruth attends uninvited, stands silently during the tribute. The beat is public myth versus private ledger, and Elodie realizing how many people are keeping the same secret from different angles.

chapters.title: What the Silence Bought
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. In a fading seaside town, Tomas tells Elodie what happened after his letter: the settlement, the NDA, his parents' relief, the slow death of his playing. He shows Elodie the one thing he kept—a recording of Elodie at fifteen, given to him by Vane as a threat disguised as a gift. The beat is complicity examined without mercy, and Elodie understanding their talent was used as collateral.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV with a long flashback. Confronting their mother with a copied letter, Elodie learns the full architecture: their mother discovered the abuse, traded Elodie's withdrawal from competition for the board burying everything, believing she was saving her child. The beat is devastating ambiguity—protection and betrayal indistinguishable—and Elodie's rage having nowhere clean to land.

chapters.title: Interlude: Hands
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, quiet chapter. Unable to decide, Elodie sits down at the conservatory's neglected rehearsal grand after hours and plays for the first time in twenty years—badly, then less badly, until dawn. A cleaning colleague, Marisol, listens from the doorway without comment. The beat is recovery of the self beneath the survivor: the music was never the wound.

chapters.title: The Necessary Aftermath
chapters.summary: Climax. Vane, alerted by a trustee, offers Elodie a settlement and the restoration of their name if the letters stay buried. Elodie instead delivers the box to the centenary memorial concert, walks onstage during the tribute, and reads the letters aloud to a stunned hall—ending with their own undelivered letter, written at fourteen and never sent. The beat is terror transfigured into testimony.

chapters.title: Owner
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Elodie's POV. Months later: the board has resigned, an independent inquiry underway, the practice wing reopened. Elodie declines interviews but accepts an invitation to teach one afternoon class a week. Playing Chopin for teenagers who don't know their history, Elodie signs the visitor log with their full name. The beat is quiet reclamation—no longer a tenant of their own life.
